proof:
The first two normals are independent since the three span and sum to zero. Use their scalar evaluations as coordinates, so the third is $-x-y$. This change of frame multiplies all areas and threshold coareas by the same positive Jacobian; thus it preserves both cap fractions and the displayed $f_i$.

For consecutive double-sector endpoints $U,V$, use coordinates $x=\xi U+\eta V$; their bridge is $\xi+\eta\le1$. If $x\in K$ lies outside the open cone and violates the bridge, then one coordinate is nonpositive. If $\eta\le0$, the segment $[x,V]$ meets the ray through $U$ at $\xi U/(1-\eta)$, strictly beyond $U$. If $\xi\le0$ use $[x,U]$ instead. Both contradict the definition of the actual endpoint. The three explicit bridges are exactly these three lines, each on the side of $0$. They contain every endpoint, and their intersection contains the piece of $K$ in each closed unique cone.

Write $X_i$ for the area captured only by cap $i$ and $Y_i$ for the double area missed by cap $i$. The two caps other than $i$ have sum $|K|-X_i+Y_i$ by counting multiplicities off the null boundary rays. Thus $X_i>Y_i$. The core triangles are contained in $K$, so $Y_1\ge at/2$, $Y_2\ge br/2$, $Y_3\ge AB/2$.

If the bridge intersection were unbounded, normalizing an unbounded sequence and taking a limit gives a nonzero recession vector. The bridge outward functional is strictly positive on every nonzero direction in its closed double cone (it equals one at both generating endpoints). The recession vector must therefore lie in an open unique cone. By cycling the normals via $(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x-y)$, take the vector to be $(s,-u)$ with $s>u>0$. The first and third bridge inequalities give $\alpha=B/A\le u/s\le1-\beta$ with $\beta=b/r$, so $0<\alpha,\beta<1$ and $\alpha+\beta\le1$.

Put $\ell=a/t$, $D_2=1-\alpha+\alpha\ell$ and $D_3=\beta+(1-\beta)\ell$, both positive. In unique sector $2$, coordinates $(x,y)=\xi(0,B)+\eta(-t,t)$, $\xi,\eta\ge0$, turn its adjacent bridges into $\xi+m\eta\le1$ and $\eta-n\xi\le1$, with $m=t(1-\alpha)/B>0$ and $n=B(1-\ell)/a$. Since the two unit points are retained, $m\le1$ and $n\ge-1$. The lines meet at $((1-m)/(1+mn),(1+n)/(1+mn))$ with $1+mn=D_2/\ell>0$. The quadrant polygon is bounded, since the first inequality has positive coefficients; its vertices are the origin, the two unit points and this intersection, allowing coincidence at an endpoint. Its physical area is $Bt(2+n-m)/(2(1+mn))$.

In unique sector $3$, use $(x,y)=(-a\xi,-b\eta)$, $\xi,\eta\ge0$. The adjacent inequalities are $\xi+v\eta\le1$ and $\eta+w\xi\le1$, where $v=(1-\ell)b/a\le1$ and $0<w=(1-\beta)a/b\le1$ by endpoint feasibility. The second inequality bounds the quadrant, and $1-vw=D_3>0$. The two lines meet at $((1-v)/D_3,(1-w)/D_3)$; the same polygon formula gives area $ab(2-v-w)/(2D_3)$. These area formulas follow by splitting at the origin into the two triangles whose determinants are the two coordinates of the intersection point. Dropping the unused bridge only enlarges each unique piece, giving
$$
X_2\le\frac{2Ba+B^2(1-\ell)-at(1-\alpha)}{2D_2},\qquad
X_3\le\frac{2ab-b^2(1-\ell)-a^2(1-\beta)}{2D_3}.
$$
Since $X_2>b^2/(2\beta)$ and $X_3>B^2/(2\alpha)$, multiply these strict comparisons by $2\beta D_2$ and $2\alpha D_3$ respectively and add:
$$
2a(\beta B+\alpha b)>\ell B^2+b^2+\beta at(1-\alpha)+\alpha a^2(1-\beta).
$$
After division by $a$ and completing squares this says
$$
0>(B-\beta t)^2/t+(b-\alpha a)^2/a+(1-\alpha-\beta)(\beta t+\alpha a),
$$
a contradiction. This is the same envelope calculation as in the double-core support-triangle source, using only endpoint feasibility, the local bridge inequalities and the core area lower bounds.

The intersection is bounded, contains a neighborhood of $0$, and has three distinct sides, each containing its prescribed positive-length bridge segment; it is a triangle. Each endpoint is retained and its bridge excludes every farther point on that ray. In a double cone its bridge restricts it to the core, and the core is included by convexity. Along the boundary of this triangle, polar angle about $0$ gives the same cyclic order as on the rays. Each of the three bridge segments is on its own side and covers exactly its double cone's angular interval. The transition between consecutive bridge segments passes through their two sides' common vertex, so the three transitions put the three vertices one each in the intervening closed unique cones. Finally b649b1adca5662b7 applies because $T$ is nondegenerate, $0$ is interior, and the three normals are spanning and balanced. It includes vertex-on-cut cases and gives the rows with exactly the area and coarea normalization stated.

statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a compact convex body with an interior mark and three spanning balanced normals whose through-mark caps each have area strictly below $|K|/2$. Translate the mark to $0$ and normalize the normals to $(1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)$. The six cyclic ray endpoints are $(A,0),(0,B),(-t,t),(-a,0),(0,-b),(r,-r)$. The three bridge halfplanes
$$
x/A+y/B\le1,\qquad x+(1-a/t)y\ge-a,\qquad y+(1-b/r)x\ge-b
$$
intersect in a nondegenerate triangle $T$ with exactly these six ray endpoints and all three original cutting chords. In each unique sector (captured by just one cap), the piece of $K$ is contained in the piece of $T$. In each double sector, the piece of $T$ is exactly the core triangle spanned by $0$ and its two ray endpoints, hence is contained in the piece of $K$. The three vertices of $T$ lie one each in the three closed unique cones. The ordinary Lorentz rows of $T$ are all at most $2$: if $k=|T|$, $Q_i$ is its cap area, $\sigma_i$ its central chord length divided by the normal length, $M=\sum_i Q_i/\sigma_i$, and $f_i=2\sqrt{kQ_i}/(\sigma_iM)$, then $f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4\le2$ for every $\{i,j,l\}=\{1,2,3\}$.
title: Canonical planar sector comparison triangle under strict half caps
